title: Knowledge Must Follow the Work
description: I am putting the architecture into software. A knowledge system has to capture what an organization does, and what it does is process.
body:
I am putting VALESKA into a working repository and a software design, not a slide. A knowledge management system is trying to capture what an organization does. What an organization does is process. Process is a value stream. If I organize the folders, the search, and the permissions by department or by subject, the collective memory will keep thinking in silos even after the shop floor has been told to think Lean. That is the problem I am building VALESKA to solve.

The work is practical: discover documents where they already live, classify them through a process framework, and make them findable by meaning — without moving the originals or dropping the access rules that belong to them.

The wrong default

In 2004, at Northrop Grumman, I watched value-stream thinking make manufacturing visible: the connected activities that turn an input into something a customer can use. Handoffs, waits, rework, and ownership showed up on the map. Enterprise content management was organized in a completely different way. Documents sat in departmental trees, topical taxonomies, or whatever folder habits people brought with them. Those structures are familiar. They do not describe how the organization produces value.

We are taught to think in functions and departments. The org chart, the library subject catalog, and the yellow pages all reward that habit. Lean asks the enterprise to break those silos. It never fails that the knowledge system leaves them standing. The result is what Lean people already know as islands of success: a process that works in one cell and cannot spread, because the collective memory is still filed by silo.

A document is not a topic. It is an artifact of work — an input, a decision, a handoff, a control, a method, or evidence of an outcome. Its place should tell you what it is for, who uses it, and what comes before and after it. That was the beginning of the Value Stream Knowledge Architecture.

From paper to something you can build

I presented the idea at Northrop Grumman as a way to connect value-stream analysis with enterprise content management. It asked people to change how they thought about information, ownership, and structure. It was too radical to become the operating model. I did not drop it. I kept developing it independently.

The early VSKA papers said the same things this repository now has to implement, in older tools. Align the architecture of the knowledge system to the process already in place, and the artifact falls into place. Most people browse; they do not search. Repeatable process structures become the road signs. Permissions should map one-to-one with that hierarchy, so security is simpler and therefore more secure. Topical trees are hard to lock down. Functional trees fight Lean. No system I had seen up to that point was structured on process.

I wrote Architexturizer in C++ so the architecture would not remain a diagram. The name was the job: give the architecture enough structure that it could be constructed, populated, and used. In Livelink that meant a programmatic way to build and load a process workspace instead of drawing folders by hand.

What I have to do now

I am taking those requirements into software we can run. A scanner discovers files across local machines, network storage, and remote systems without claiming ownership of the originals. Metadata extraction gives each record an identity: path, owner, time, type. APQC classification attaches the record to a common process framework instead of a private folder dialect. Embeddings let people find by meaning as well as by filename. PostgreSQL and pgvector hold that index. Permissions stay with the record. A useful result is not a document that merely matches a query. It is a document still connected to its source, its owner, its location, and its access rules.

Alfresco is the planned home for browsing and search, because a knowledge architecture has to live inside the systems where records already live. VALESKA should make that landscape intelligible. It should not demand that an organization abandon it.

There is a working question hanging over this first commit. Can a process taxonomy, applied to files we do not move, actually improve findability without breaking the permission model those files already have? Classification must be reviewable. Retrieval must be tested against real collections. Until those tests are run, this is a design we can execute, not a claim that the collective already thinks in process.

A beginning, not the invention

I am not inventing the idea today. I am beginning the next chapter: a searchable implementation that still follows the work. The insight is still the value-stream work I could not leave alone. I developed the process, the vocabulary, and the security model in the VSKA papers. This repository is how I start to run it.

Historical basis: VALESKA initial repository commit be8a50a, August 8, 2025; VALESKA_SDD.md. The Northrop and Architexturizer material is David Gargan’s firsthand account, with early VSKA documents retained as supporting artifacts.
